claim: From genetic screens in C. elegans, splicing factor RNP-6/PUF60 was identified whose activity suppresses immunity but promotes longevity.
source: From genetic screens in C. elegans, we identified splicing factor RNP-6/PUF60 whose activity suppresses immunity, but promotes longevity, suggesting a tradeoff between these processes.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript including survival assays and lifespan measurements.

claim: Bacterial pathogen exposure affects gene expression in a rnp-6 dependent manner.
source: Bacterial pathogen exposure affects gene expression and splicing in a rnp-6 dependent manner, and rnp-6 gain and loss-of-function activities reveal an active role in immune regulation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data comparing wildtype and rnp-6 mutant animals under infection conditions, showing differential gene expression patterns.

claim: Bacterial pathogen exposure affects splicing in a rnp-6 dependent manner.
source: Bacterial pathogen exposure affects gene expression and splicing in a rnp-6 dependent manner, and rnp-6 gain and loss-of-function activities reveal an active role in immune regulation.
evidence: This is supported by splicing analysis showing that infection-induced alternative splicing events are altered in rnp-6 mutants.

claim: Another longevity promoting splicing factor, SFA-1, exerts an immuno-suppressive effect.
source: Another longevity promoting splicing factor, SFA-1, similarly exerts an immuno-suppressive effect, working downstream or parallel to RNP-6.
evidence: This is supported by infection survival experiments showing that SFA-1 overexpression compromises survival upon bacterial infection.

claim: SFA-1 works downstream or parallel to RNP-6.
source: Another longevity promoting splicing factor, SFA-1, similarly exerts an immuno-suppressive effect, working downstream or parallel to RNP-6.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing that sfa-1 knockdown suppresses rnp-6 mutant phenotypes.

claim: RNP-6 acts through TIR-1/PMK-1/MAPK signaling to modulate immunity.
source: RNP-6 acts through TIR-1/PMK-1/MAPK signaling to modulate immunity.
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis experiments showing that rnp-6 RNAi effects require pmk-1 and tir-1, and by western blot data showing rnp-6 affects PMK-1 phosphorylation.

claim: The mammalian homolog PUF60 displays anti-inflammatory properties.
source: The mammalian homolog, PUF60, also displays anti-inflammatory properties, and its levels swiftly decrease after bacterial infection in mammalian cells, implying a role in the host response.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in mammalian cells showing that PUF60 overexpression reduces cytokine expression upon infection.

claim: PUF60 levels decrease after bacterial infection in mammalian cells.
source: The mammalian homolog, PUF60, also displays anti-inflammatory properties, and its levels swiftly decrease after bacterial infection in mammalian cells, implying a role in the host response.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data showing reduced PUF60 protein and transcript levels after S. aureus infection in HeLa, MEF, and RAW264.7 cells.

claim: The MAPK cascade of NSY-1-SEK-1-PMK-1 is essential to innate immunity in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, the MAPK cascade of NSY-1-SEK-1-PMK-1 is essential to innate immunity, and has orthologs in mammals (ASK1 MAPKKK-MKK3/6 MAPKK-p38 MAPK pathway) playing a similar role (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2002.

claim: The C. elegans MAPK cascade has orthologs in mammals (ASK1 MAPKKK-MKK3/6 MAPKK-p38 MAPK pathway) playing a similar role.
source: In C. elegans, the MAPK cascade of NSY-1-SEK-1-PMK-1 is essential to innate immunity, and has orthologs in mammals (ASK1 MAPKKK-MKK3/6 MAPKK-p38 MAPK pathway) playing a similar role (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2002.

claim: MAPK signaling in C. elegans depends on TIR-1, a Toll-Interleukin-1 Receptor (TIR) domain protein and an ortholog of mammalian SARM.
source: This signaling in C. elegans depends on TIR-1, a Toll-Interleukin-1 Receptor (TIR) domain protein and an ortholog of mammalian SARM (Couillault et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Couillault et al., 2004.

claim: Deletion mutants of the C. elegans PMK-1 pathway exhibit dysregulated transcriptional responses and hypersensitivity to infection challenge.
source: Deletion mutants of the C. elegans PMK-1 pathway correspondingly exhibit dysregulated transcriptional responses and hypersensitivity to infection challenge (Fletcher et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2002; Troemel et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fletcher et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2002; Troemel et al., 2006.

claim: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), such as Toll-like-receptors, do not appear to play a significant role in C. elegans infection responses.
source: Evidently, pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), such as Toll-like-receptors, which function upstream to control the MAPK pathway in mammals and insects, do not appear to play a significant role in C. elegans infection responses (Pujol et al., 2001; Pukkila-Worley and Ausubel, 2012), but rather mediate the aversive behavioral response to pathogens (Brandt and Ringstad, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pujol et al., 2001; Pukkila-Worley and Ausubel, 2012.

claim: Pattern recognition receptors mediate the aversive behavioral response to pathogens in C. elegans.
source: Evidently, pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), such as Toll-like-receptors, which function upstream to control the MAPK pathway in mammals and insects, do not appear to play a significant role in C. elegans infection responses (Pujol et al., 2001; Pukkila-Worley and Ausubel, 2012), but rather mediate the aversive behavioral response to pathogens (Brandt and Ringstad, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brandt and Ringstad, 2015.

claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) play an important role in controlling the MAPK pathway in C. elegans in the context of infection.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) apparently play an important role in controlling the MAPK pathway in C. elegans in the context of infection (Styer et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2011; Zugasti et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Styer et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2011; Zugasti et al., 2014.

claim: The ligand for dcar-1 was identified to be an endogenous molecule, 4-hydroxyphenyllactic acid (HPLA).
source: However, identities of the actual ligands during infection for these receptors are not clear except for dcar-1, whose ligand was identified to be an endogenous molecule, 4-hydroxyphenyllactic acid (HPLA) (Zugasti et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zugasti et al., 2014.

claim: Various physiological processes are regulated by splicing in C. elegans, including heavy metal resistance, metabolism and lifespan.
source: Various physiological processes are regulated by splicing in C. elegans, including heavy metal resistance, metabolism and lifespan (Heintz et al., 2017; Tabrez et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019a), yet how splicing affects innate immunity, especially in invertebrate models, remains relatively unexplored.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heintz et al., 2017; Tabrez et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019a.

claim: 2°C cold stress rapidly killed C. elegans wildtype N2 animals.
source: We observed that 2°C cold stress rapidly killed C. elegans wildtype N2 animals (Figure 1A), while long-lived strains such as daf-2/InsR and eat-2 dietary restriction mutants were remarkably resistant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Long-lived strains such as daf-2/InsR and eat-2 dietary restriction mutants were remarkably resistant to 2°C cold stress.
source: We observed that 2°C cold stress rapidly killed C. elegans wildtype N2 animals (Figure 1A), while long-lived strains such as daf-2/InsR and eat-2 dietary restriction mutants were remarkably resistant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Two screenings were conducted with 16000 haploid genomes screened for cold resistance.
source: Two screenings were conducted with 16000 haploid genomes screened.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the genetic screen.

claim: A total of 303 cold resistant mutants were recovered from the genetic screen.
source: A total of 303 cold resistant mutants were recovered.
evidence: This describes the results of the genetic screen.

claim: A novel mutation in rnp-6 was identified from the cold resistance screen, which encodes an ortholog of the mammalian splicing factor Poly(U) Binding Splicing Factor 60 (PUF60).
source: From the screen, we identified a novel mutation in rnp-6, which encodes an ortholog of the mammalian splicing factor Poly(U) Binding Splicing Factor 60 (PUF60).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing and genetic mapping data.

claim: PUF60 facilitates the association of the U2 snRNP with target RNA molecules.
source: PUF60 facilitates the association of the U2 snRNP with target RNA molecules (Page-McCaw et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Page-McCaw et al., 1999.

claim: PUF60 is essential, and heterozygous loss of function causes Verheij syndrome.
source: PUF60 is essential, and heterozygous loss of function causes Verheij syndrome, which is characterized by severe developmental abnormalities in most patients (Low et al., 2017; Verheij et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Low et al., 2017; Verheij et al., 2009.

claim: PUF60 is involved in Hepatitis B virus infection.
source: PUF60 is also involved in Hepatitis B virus infection (Sun et al., 2017) and cancer progression (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2017.

claim: PUF60 is involved in cancer progression.
source: PUF60 is also involved in Hepatitis B virus infection (Sun et al., 2017) and cancer progression (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2019.

claim: A G281D amino acid substitution in rnp-6 lies within the second RNA binding motif at a position conserved across evolution.
source: In C. elegans, we found a G281D amino acid substitution in rnp-6 lying within the second RNA binding motif at a position conserved across evolution (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The rnp-6 G281D mutation confers no obvious developmental phenotypes, despite rnp-6 null mutants being embryonic lethal.
source: Surprisingly, this mutation confers no obvious developmental phenotypes, despite rnp-6 null mutants being embryonic lethal (Johnsen et al., 2000).
evidence: The observation of no obvious developmental phenotypes is from the current study, while the lethality of null mutants is supported by citation to Johnsen et al., 2000.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1124) mutant was highly resistant to cold stress.
source: Upon outcrossing the original mutant, rnp-6(dh1124) was highly resistant to cold stress (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: An independent CRISPR line carrying the same rnp-6 G281D mutation (dh1127) showed the same cold resistance phenotype.
source: An independent line carrying the same mutation (dh1127) was created using CRISPR gene editing, which showed the same phenotype, confirming the casual relation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant had a slightly reduced brood size.
source: The mutant had a slightly reduced brood size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), a slight but significant developmental delay (around 3.5 hr more to reach adulthood) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and a marginally shorter body size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), but did not significantly affect pharyngeal pumping rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant had a slight but significant developmental delay (around 3.5 hr more to reach adulthood).
source: The mutant had a slightly reduced brood size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), a slight but significant developmental delay (around 3.5 hr more to reach adulthood) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and a marginally shorter body size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), but did not significantly affect pharyngeal pumping rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant had a marginally shorter body size.
source: The mutant had a slightly reduced brood size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), a slight but significant developmental delay (around 3.5 hr more to reach adulthood) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and a marginally shorter body size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), but did not significantly affect pharyngeal pumping rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by body length data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant did not significantly affect pharyngeal pumping rate.
source: The mutant had a slightly reduced brood size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), a slight but significant developmental delay (around 3.5 hr more to reach adulthood) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and a marginally shorter body size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), but did not significantly affect pharyngeal pumping rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by pharyngeal pumping rate data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant was resistant to heat stress.
source: Interestingly, the mutant was also resistant to heat stress (Figure 1F) and oxidative stress (Figure 1G), suggesting this mutation widely confers resistance to multiple abiotic stresses.
evidence: This is supported by heat stress survival data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant was resistant to oxidative stress.
source: Interestingly, the mutant was also resistant to heat stress (Figure 1F) and oxidative stress (Figure 1G), suggesting this mutation widely confers resistance to multiple abiotic stresses.
evidence: This is supported by oxidative stress survival data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: C. elegans mutants that are resistant to abiotic stresses often have better survival upon infectious insults and are long-lived.
source: C. elegans mutants that are resistant to abiotic stresses often have better survival upon infectious insults and are long-lived (Garsin et al., 2003; TeKippe and Aballay, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Garsin et al., 2003; TeKippe and Aballay, 2010.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant was more sensitive to S. aureus infection.
source: Unexpectedly, this mutant was more sensitive to all pathogenic bacteria tested (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant was more sensitive to E. faecalis infection.
source: Unexpectedly, this mutant was more sensitive to all pathogenic bacteria tested (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant was more sensitive to P. aeruginosa infection.
source: Unexpectedly, this mutant was more sensitive to all pathogenic bacteria tested (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The infection sensitivity phenotype of rnp-6(dh1127) was confirmed with another independently created CRISPR line (dh1125).
source: This phenotype was confirmed with another independently created CRISPR line (dh1125) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant displayed the same sensitive phenotype on full lawn S. aureus plates.
source: We also performed the experiments on full lawn S. aureus plates. The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant displayed the same sensitive phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), suggesting the sensitivity was not due to differential bacterial exposure.
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: There was no difference in bacterial burden between wildtype and rnp-6(dh1127) animals infected with S. aureus.
source: Although rnp-6(dh1127) animals were more sensitive to S. aureus, we did not observe a difference in bacterial burden (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant showed robust longevity at 20°C when cultured with E. coli OP50.
source: Interestingly, when cultured with the weakly pathogenic E. coli strain OP50, the rnp-6(dh1127) mutant showed robust longevity at 20°C (Figure 1K) and a normal lifespan at 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J), indicating the shortened survival on pathogenic bacteria was specific and unlikely due to general sickness of the mutant.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant showed a normal lifespan at 25°C when cultured with E. coli OP50.
source: Interestingly, when cultured with the weakly pathogenic E. coli strain OP50, the rnp-6(dh1127) mutant showed robust longevity at 20°C (Figure 1K) and a normal lifespan at 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J), indicating the shortened survival on pathogenic bacteria was specific and unlikely due to general sickness of the mutant.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The rnp-6(dh1127) mutant was sensitive to pathogenic bacterial infection at both 20°C and 25°C.
source: Although longevity is dependent on temperature, the mutant was sensitive to pathogenic bacterial infection at both 20°C and 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: No significant changes in RNP-6 transcript levels could be detected after S. aureus infection in C. elegans.
source: We performed qRT-PCR and western blots to detect the endogenous levels of RNP-6 at both transcript and protein levels. However, no significant changes could be detected after S. aureus infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L,M).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1L.

claim: No significant changes in RNP-6 protein levels could be detected after S. aureus infection in C. elegans.
source: We performed qRT-PCR and western blots to detect the endogenous levels of RNP-6 at both transcript and protein levels. However, no significant changes could be detected after S. aureus infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L,M).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1M.

claim: The rnp-6 G281D mutation led to 1483 differentially expressed genes under non-infected conditions.
source: The rnp-6 G281D mutation led to numerous differentially expressed genes (DEGs) under both non-infected (1483 genes) (Figure 2—source data 1) and infected conditions (1707 genes) (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data comparing wildtype and rnp-6 mutant animals.

claim: The rnp-6 G281D mutation led to 1707 differentially expressed genes under infected conditions.
source: The rnp-6 G281D mutation led to numerous differentially expressed genes (DEGs) under both non-infected (1483 genes) (Figure 2—source data 1) and infected conditions (1707 genes) (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data comparing wildtype and rnp-6 mutant animals under infection.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes in rnp-6 mutants revealed an enrichment of genes implicated in immunity under both non-infected and infected conditions.
source: Under both conditions, Gene Ontology (GO) term analysis of the DEGs revealed an enrichment of genes implicated in immunity (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: 662 genes were found to be induced by S. aureus infection in the N2 background.
source: 662 genes were found to be induced by S. aureus infection in the N2 background.
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing data comparing infected and non-infected wildtype animals.

claim: For 116 genes induced by S. aureus infection, the expression was dampened in the rnp-6 mutant under infection.
source: For 116 of them, the expression was dampened in the rnp-6 mutant under infection (Figure 2C) (Figure 2—source data 3), and these rnp-6 dependent infection induced genes were enriched for immune response genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: rnp-6 dependent infection induced genes were enriched for immune response genes.
source: For 116 of them, the expression was dampened in the rnp-6 mutant under infection (Figure 2C) (Figure 2—source data 3), and these rnp-6 dependent infection induced genes were enriched for immune response genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 1536 genes were repressed by S. aureus infection in wildtype animals.
source: Conversely, 1536 genes were repressed by S. aureus infection, and the expression remained higher in the rnp-6 mutant for 159 of them (Figure 2D) (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing data comparing infected and non-infected wildtype animals.

claim: For 159 genes repressed by S. aureus infection, the expression remained higher in the rnp-6 mutant.
source: Conversely, 1536 genes were repressed by S. aureus infection, and the expression remained higher in the rnp-6 mutant for 159 of them (Figure 2D) (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Among rnp-6 dependent infection repressed genes, metabolic genes appeared to be highly enriched.
source: Among these rnp-6 dependent infection repressed genes, metabolic genes appeared to be highly enriched (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The most enriched GO terms among rnp-6 dependent infection repressed genes included organic acid metabolic process and fatty acid metabolic process.
source: The most enriched GO terms included organic acid metabolic process and fatty acid metabolic process (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: rnp-6 G281D substitution compromises induction of antimicrobial genes (nlp-30, nlp-34, spp-1 and ilys-2) upon S. aureus infection.
source: Consistent with the results from RNA sequencing, infection induced expression of antimicrobial proteins (nlp-30, nlp-34 and spp-1) and lysozyme (ilys-2) was severely compromised by rnp-6 G281D substitution (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Metabolic genes (nhr-62, nhr-3, cth-1 and fat-5), which are suppressed in wildtype animals upon infection, maintain a higher expression in the rnp-6(dh1127) mutant.
source: On the other hand, the expression of nuclear hormone receptors (nhr-62 and nhr-3) and metabolic enzymes (cth-1 and fat-5) was refractory to the repression by infection in the rnp-6 G281D mutant (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 83 genes were found to be alternatively spliced upon S. aureus infection in wildtype animals.
source: 83 genes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1) were found to be alternatively spliced upon S. aureus infection in wildtype animals.
evidence: This is supported by splicing analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 456 genes showed alternative splicing when comparing infected wildtype animals and infected rnp-6(dh1127) mutants.
source: When comparing infected wildtype animals and infected rnp-6(dh1127) mutants, we found a larger number of alternatively spliced genes (456 genes) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by splicing analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Over half of the genes (43 out of 83) showing infection induced alternative splicing were also altered in the infected rnp-6(dh1127) mutants when compared to infected wildtype N2 animals.
source: Over half of the genes (43 out of 83) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 3) showing infection induced alternative splicing, were also altered in the infected rnp-6(dh1127) mutants when compared to infected wildtype N2 animals.
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In wildtype animals, S. aureus infection induced splicing events were predominated by 'cassette exon' (44.9%) and 'retained intron' (22.4%).
source: In wildtype animals, S. aureus infection induced splicing events were predominated by 'cassette exon' (44.9%) and 'retained intron' (22.4%). This was also true when we compared infected rnp-6(1127) mutants with infected wildtype animals ('cassette exon' 59.5%, 'retained intron' 15.2%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by SAJR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When comparing infected rnp-6(dh1127) mutants with infected wildtype animals, splicing events were predominated by 'cassette exon' (59.5%) and 'retained intron' (15.2%).
source: In wildtype animals, S. aureus infection induced splicing events were predominated by 'cassette exon' (44.9%) and 'retained intron' (22.4%). This was also true when we compared infected rnp-6(1127) mutants with infected wildtype animals ('cassette exon' 59.5%, 'retained intron' 15.2%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by SAJR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S. aureus infection enhanced intron one splicing in prg-2 in wildtype animals, but this effect was substantially suppressed in the rnp-6(dh1127) mutants.
source: S. aureus infection enhanced intron one splicing in prg-2 in wildtype animals, but this effect was substantially suppressed in the rnp-6(dh1127) mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and agarose gel analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Infection led to inclusion of exon 6 and exon 7 of gyg-1, and this effect was largely suppressed by the G281D substitution in the dh1127 mutants.
source: Infection also led to inclusion of exon 6 and exon 7 of gyg-1, and again this effect was largely suppressed by the G281D substitution in the dh1127 mutants (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and agarose gel analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Infection increased the abundance of the short tos-1 isoform in wildtype animals.
source: Further, infection increased the abundance of the short tos-1 isoform in wildtype animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and agarose gel analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The rnp-6 G281D mutants had an increased longer to shorter isoform ratio of tos-1 under non-infected condition, and this ratio remained the same after infection.
source: Intriguingly, the rnp-6 G281D mutants had an increased longer to shorter isoform ratio under non-infected condition, and this ratio remained the same after infection (Figure 3D), suggesting it is refractory to input.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and agarose gel analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: RNAi knockdown of rnp-6 resulted in a robust extension of survival upon S. aureus infection.
source: Surprisingly, RNAi knockdown of rnp-6 resulted in a robust extension of survival upon S. aureus infection (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RNAi against rnp-6 conferred enhanced survival on full lawn S. aureus plates.
source: To test whether the survival phenotype of rnp-6 RNAi is due to reduced exposure to bacteria, we repeated the survival experiment using full lawn plates on which bacterial avoidance is impossible. RNAi against rnp-6 still conferred enhanced survival under these conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), ruling out the possibility that the phenotype is caused by differential bacterial exposure.
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: rnp-6 RNAi did not affect S. aureus bacterial burden.
source: Further, rnp-6 RNAi did not affect S. aureus bacterial burden, suggesting the survival phenotype is caused by independent mechanisms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: rnp-6 RNAi strongly induced the expression of numerous infection responsive genes, including nlp-34, lys-3, irg-2, irg-1, M01G12.9, fmo-2 and cyp-37B1.
source: Consistent with the survival results, rnp-6 RNAi strongly induced the expression of numerous infection responsive genes, including nlp-34, lys-3, irg-2, irg-1, M01G12.9, fmo-2 and cyp-37B1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: rnp-6 RNAi promoted the splicing of prg-2 intron-1.
source: Notably, rnp-6 RNAi promoted the splicing of prg-2 intron-1 (Figure 4C), which shows the same trend as seen during infection and is largely inhibited by the G281D mutation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and agarose gel analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: rnp-6 RNAi increased the relative abundance of the longer isoform of tos-1.
source: On the other hand, rnp-6 RNAi increased the relative abundance of the longer isoform of tos-1 (Figure 4D), which more resembles the change induced by the G281D mutation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and agarose gel analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Overexpressing RNP-6 greatly compromised infection survival upon S. aureus exposure.
source: Furthermore, overexpressing RNP-6 greatly compromised infection survival upon S. aureus (Figure 4E) and E. faecalis exposure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F), but promoted longevity at 25°C when the animals were cultured with the weakly pathogenic E. coli OP50 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Overexpressing RNP-6 compromised infection survival upon E. faecalis exposure.
source: Furthermore, overexpressing RNP-6 greatly compromised infection survival upon S. aureus (Figure 4E) and E. faecalis exposure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F), but promoted longevity at 25°C when the animals were cultured with the weakly pathogenic E. coli OP50 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Overexpressing RNP-6 promoted longevity at 25°C when the animals were cultured with E. coli OP50.
source: Furthermore, overexpressing RNP-6 greatly compromised infection survival upon S. aureus (Figure 4E) and E. faecalis exposure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F), but promoted longevity at 25°C when the animals were cultured with the weakly pathogenic E. coli OP50 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The sensitivity phenotype of the RNP-6 overexpressing strain is not due to differential bacterial exposure on full lawns.
source: The sensitivity phenotype of the RNP-6 overexpressing strain is not due to differential bacterial exposure, since the phenotype was still manifest on full lawns (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Overexpression of RNP-6 did not have an observable effect on bacterial burden in S. aureus infected C. elegans.
source: Also, overexpression of RNP-6 did not have an observable effect on bacterial burden in S. aureus infected C. elegans (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: rnp-6 dependent infection responsive genes were significantly enriched for PMK-1 target genes.
source: Interestingly, we found that the rnp-6 dependent infection responsive genes were significantly enriched for PMK-1 target genes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Among the 116 RNP-6 dependent infection induced genes, 17 were also PMK-1 dependent.
source: Among the 116 RNP-6 dependent infection induced genes (Figure 2C), 17 were also PMK-1 dependent (Bond et al., 2014; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published PMK-1 dependent genes from Bond et al., 2014.

claim: For the 159 genes whose repression by infection was reverted by the rnp-6 G281D substitution, 55 of them were also up-regulated in the pmk-1 deletion mutant.
source: For the 159 genes whose repression by infection was reverted by the rnp-6 G281D substitution (Figure 2D), 55 of them were also up-regulated in the pmk-1 deletion mutant (Mertenskötter et al., 2013; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published pmk-1 mutant data from Mertenskötter et al., 2013.

claim: Deletion of pmk-1 completely abolished the beneficial effect of rnp-6 RNAi on infection survival.
source: Knocking down rnp-6 increased the animals' survival upon S. aureus infection, and deletion of pmk-1 or its upstream activator tir-1 completely abolished the beneficial effect of rnp-6 reduction (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Deletion of tir-1 completely abolished the beneficial effect of rnp-6 RNAi on infection survival.
source: Knocking down rnp-6 increased the animals' survival upon S. aureus infection, and deletion of pmk-1 or its upstream activator tir-1 completely abolished the beneficial effect of rnp-6 reduction (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Deletion of daf-16/FOXO had no effect on the rnp-6 RNAi extended survival upon infection.
source: By contrast, deletions of daf-16/FOXO or hlh-30/TFEB, which are also important regulators of innate immunity (Garsin et al., 2003; Visvikis et al., 2014), had no and minimal effects on the rnp-6 RNAi extended survival, respectively (53.6% increase in N2% and 43.4% increase in hlh30(tm1978), area under survival curves) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Deletion of hlh-30/TFEB had minimal effects on the rnp-6 RNAi extended survival upon infection.
source: By contrast, deletions of daf-16/FOXO or hlh-30/TFEB, which are also important regulators of innate immunity (Garsin et al., 2003; Visvikis et al., 2014), had no and minimal effects on the rnp-6 RNAi extended survival, respectively (53.6% increase in N2% and 43.4% increase in hlh30(tm1978), area under survival curves) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Overexpressing RNP-6 did not further enhance sensitivity in the pmk-1 deletion background upon S. aureus infection.
source: Overexpressing RNP-6 or G281D substitution rendered the animals susceptible to S. aureus infection in wildtype background, but did not further enhance sensitivity in the pmk-1 deletion background (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The rnp-6 G281D substitution did not further enhance sensitivity in the pmk-1 deletion background upon S. aureus infection.
source: Overexpressing RNP-6 or G281D substitution rendered the animals susceptible to S. aureus infection in wildtype background, but did not further enhance sensitivity in the pmk-1 deletion background (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The rnp-6 G281D substitution did not further sensitize the pmk-1 deletion mutant under P. aeruginosa infection conditions.
source: The rnp-6 G281D substitution also did not further sensitize the pmk-1 deletion mutant under P. aeruginosa infection conditions (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Upon RNAi knockdown of rnp-6, there was a significant increase in phospho-PMK-1.
source: Upon RNAi knockdown of rnp-6, we observed a significant increase in phospho-PMK-1 (Figure 5G), suggesting PMK-1 activity increases upon rnp-6 reduction.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: No reproducible difference in splicing patterns or expression levels of PMK-1 MAPK signaling components was observed comparing wildtype and rnp-6(dh1127) animals under non-infected or S. aureus infected conditions.
source: However, we did not observe any reproducible difference in splicing patterns or expression levels of PMK-1 MAPK signaling components comparing wildtype and rnp-6(dh1127) animals under non-infected or S. aureus infected conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–I; Figure 2—source data 1 and 2), suggesting that rnp-6 regulates this pathway via other mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–I.

claim: Overexpressing splicing factor SFA-1 resulted in robust longevity under non-infected conditions.
source: Overexpressing splicing factor SFA-1 resulted in robust longevity under non-infected conditions (Figure 6A), as previously reported (Heintz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6A and citation to Heintz et al., 2017.

claim: SFA-1 overexpression severely compromised survival upon S. aureus infection.
source: However, similar to rnp-6, SFA-1 overexpression severely compromised survival upon S. aureus (Figure 6B) and E. faecalis infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SFA-1 overexpression severely compromised survival upon E. faecalis infection.
source: However, similar to rnp-6, SFA-1 overexpression severely compromised survival upon S. aureus (Figure 6B) and E. faecalis infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNAi knockdown of sfa-1 increased infection survival in wildtype worms.
source: Moreover, RNAi knockdown of sfa-1 not only increased infection survival in wildtype worms (Figure 6C), but also completely suppressed infection sensitivity of the G281D mutant of rnp-6 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RNAi knockdown of sfa-1 completely suppressed infection sensitivity of the G281D mutant of rnp-6.
source: Moreover, RNAi knockdown of sfa-1 not only increased infection survival in wildtype worms (Figure 6C), but also completely suppressed infection sensitivity of the G281D mutant of rnp-6 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SFA-1 overexpression did not further increase rnp-6 G281D longevity when animals were cultured with E. coli OP50.
source: Consistent with a strong interaction, SFA-1 overexpression did not further increase rnp-6 G281D longevity when animals were cultured with E. coli OP50 (Figure 6E), and knocking down sfa-1 completely suppressed rnp-6 G281D longevity (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Knocking down sfa-1 completely suppressed rnp-6 G281D longevity.
source: Consistent with a strong interaction, SFA-1 overexpression did not further increase rnp-6 G281D longevity when animals were cultured with E. coli OP50 (Figure 6E), and knocking down sfa-1 completely suppressed rnp-6 G281D longevity (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Knocking-down repo-1 only partially rescued the infection sensitivity caused by rnp-6 G281D mutation.
source: By contrast, knocking-down repo-1, which is also implicated in longevity (Heintz et al., 2017), only partially rescued the infection sensitivity caused by rnp-6 G281D mutation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), while hrpu-1 knockdown had little effect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: hrpu-1 knockdown had little effect on the infection sensitivity caused by rnp-6 G281D mutation.
source: By contrast, knocking-down repo-1, which is also implicated in longevity (Heintz et al., 2017), only partially rescued the infection sensitivity caused by rnp-6 G281D mutation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), while hrpu-1 knockdown had little effect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No obvious co-immunoprecipitation of RNP-6 with SFA-1 was detected.
source: However, we saw no obvious co-immunoprecipitation of RNP-6 with SFA-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The sensitivity caused by SFA-1 overexpression was not additive to that of pmk-1 deletion.
source: We also observed that the sensitivity caused by SFA-1 overexpression was not additive to that of pmk-1 deletion (Figure 6G), supporting the idea of sfa-1 and pmk-1 working in the same pathway, similar to that of rnp-6.
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Knocking-down sfa-1 induced phosphorylation of PMK-1.
source: Next, we tested whether sfa-1 also exerts inhibitory effects on PMK-1 activity. Knocking-down sfa-1 also induced phosphorylation of PMK-1 (Figure 6H), indicating that sfa-1 similarly restrains PMK-1 activation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: sfa-1 RNAi was able to increase infection survival in pmk-1 deletion mutants.
source: In contrast to rnp-6 RNAi, however, sfa-1 RNAi was able to increase infection survival in pmk-1 deletion mutants (Figure 6I), suggesting sfa-1 also moderates immunity via pmk-1 independent pathways.
evidence: This is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: S. aureus infection reduced PUF60 protein levels in HeLa cells, MEF cells, and RAW264.7 macrophage-like cells.
source: We infected human epithelial HeLa cells, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) and RAW264.7 macrophage-like cells with S. aureus and observed a sharp reduction of PUF60 protein levels in all three cell types (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: S. aureus infection reduced PUF60 transcript levels in mammalian cells.
source: S. aureus infection also reduced PUF60 transcript levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reduction of PUF60 by siRNA was sufficient to drive expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-8, CXCL2, and IL-1α in HeLa cells.
source: Interestingly, reduction of PUF60 alone was sufficient to drive expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, namely IL-6, IL-8, CXCL2, IL-1α (Figure 7B), IL-18 and CCL5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), but had no effects on anti-inflammatory gene TGF-β1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Reduction of PUF60 by siRNA was sufficient to drive expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-18 and CCL5 in HeLa cells.
source: Interestingly, reduction of PUF60 alone was sufficient to drive expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, namely IL-6, IL-8, CXCL2, IL-1α (Figure 7B), IL-18 and CCL5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), but had no effects on anti-inflammatory gene TGF-β1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reduction of PUF60 by siRNA had no effects on anti-inflammatory gene TGF-β1 in HeLa cells.
source: Interestingly, reduction of PUF60 alone was sufficient to drive expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, namely IL-6, IL-8, CXCL2, IL-1α (Figure 7B), IL-18 and CCL5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), but had no effects on anti-inflammatory gene TGF-β1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A moderate induction of cytokines was observed upon PUF60 knockdown in RAW264.7 macrophage-like cells.
source: We also observed a moderate induction of the same cytokines upon PUF60 knockdown in RAW264.7 macrophage-like cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) despite the relatively low RNAi efficiency of PUF60 in this cell line (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Overexpression of wildtype PUF60 exerted moderate inhibitory effects on cytokine induction but the effects were not statistically significant.
source: Overexpression of wildtype PUF60 also exerted moderate inhibitory effects on cytokine induction but the effects were not statistically significant (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Overexpression of wildtype or the mutated form of PUF60 improved HeLa cell survival upon S. aureus infection at 24 hr post-infection.
source: Also, overexpression of wildtype or the mutated form of PUF60 improved HeLa cell survival upon S. aureus infection at a later time point (post-infection 24 hr) (Figure 7D) without affecting bacterial internalization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Overexpression of PUF60 did not affect bacterial internalization in HeLa cells.
source: Also, overexpression of wildtype or the mutated form of PUF60 improved HeLa cell survival upon S. aureus infection at a later time point (post-infection 24 hr) (Figure 7D) without affecting bacterial internalization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Viruses commonly interact with the host splicing machinery.
source: Viruses commonly interact with the host splicing machinery, whereas not much is known regarding bacterial interference with host RNA splicing (Chauhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chauhan et al., 2019.

claim: Not much is known regarding bacterial interference with host RNA splicing.
source: Viruses commonly interact with the host splicing machinery, whereas not much is known regarding bacterial interference with host RNA splicing (Chauhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chauhan et al., 2019.

claim: MyD88, a Toll-like-receptor signaling adaptor and an analog of tir-1 in mammals, is controlled by alternative mRNA splicing.
source: In support of the latter idea, MyD88, a Toll-like-receptor signaling adaptor and an analog (functionally similar but differ significantly at the sequence level) of tir-1 in mammals, is controlled by alternative mRNA splicing (De Arras and Alper, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to De Arras and Alper, 2013.

claim: Splicing acts downstream of dietary restriction to promote longevity.
source: Splicing acts downstream of dietary restriction to promote longevity (Heintz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heintz et al., 2017.

claim: Aberrant activation of PMK-1 causes toxicity and shorter lifespan in C. elegans.
source: Aberrant activation of PMK-1 causes toxicity and shorter lifespan in C. elegans (Cheesman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cheesman et al., 2016.

claim: In both dietary restricted animals and daf-2 mutants, PMK-1 MAPK signaling is inhibited.
source: Also, in both dietary restricted animals and daf-2 mutants, PMK-1 MAPK signaling is inhibited (Wu et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2019b.

claim: Hypomorphic mutations of PUF60 are known to cause a rare genetic disease called Verheij syndrome.
source: Hypomorphic mutations of PUF60 are known to cause a rare genetic disease called Verheij syndrome (Abdin et al., 2018; El Chehadeh et al., 2017; Verheij et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abdin et al., 2018; El Chehadeh et al., 2017; Verheij et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2018.

claim: A reduction of PUF60 activity may trigger inflammation, which could be one of the drivers of the pathology in Verheij syndrome.
source: Our results suggest a reduction of PUF60 activity may trigger inflammation, which could be one of the drivers of the pathology.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PUF60 knockdown induces pro-inflammatory cytokines and the knowledge that Verheij syndrome is caused by hypomorphic PUF60 mutations.

claim: The function of RNP-6/PUF60 in suppressing immunity is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Altogether our findings demonstrate an evolutionarily conserved modulation of immunity by specific components of the splicing machinery.
evidence: This is supported by data showing similar immunosuppressive effects of RNP-6 in C. elegans and PUF60 in mammalian cells.
